title: Devarim: pass by gently (Deuteronomy 2:4–9)
hook: Israel must pass Edom and Moab without taking their land

segments.voice: Yesterday, the scouts retold, Moses' own part included. Your line was tell it so it won't repeat. Did you pass one hard lesson on? Today, a march past other people's land. Day four hundred eighty-six.

Imagine a huge crowd on the move, hungry, tired of the desert, and suddenly strong. Ahead of them is a green country with wells and towns, and the people who live there are, the text says, afraid of them. Every story you know says what happens next. The big crowd takes what it wants. Moses remembers the order that came instead. Walk past. Pay for your water. Don't take a single footstep of their land. It's one of the quieter moments of his farewell, and one of the strangest for an army.
screen: `A STRONG CROWD, A GREEN COUNTRY.` → `THEY ARE AFRAID OF YOU.` → `WALK PAST.`

segments.voice: The first neighbors are the children of Esau in Seir, the people of Edom. Moses calls them your brothers, because Esau was Jacob's twin. God's instruction, as Moses retells it: they'll be afraid of you, so take good care of yourselves, and don't start a fight. I won't give you any of their land, not even enough to set the sole of your foot on, because I gave Mount Seir to Esau. Buy food from them with money, and buy water to drink. And then a line that sounds almost like a parent: "these forty years the LORD thy God hath been with thee; thou hast lacked nothing." In other words, you don't need what's theirs. You never did. Then Moab, the descendants of Lot, Abraham's nephew. Same rule. Don't harass them, don't go to war, their land was given to them too. Notice what that means. In this telling, the God who promised Israel a land also gave other peoples their lands, and expects Israel to honor the boundary even when it could be crossed easily. Numbers remembers that Edom actually refused Israel passage, and Israel went around. Deuteronomy doesn't dwell on the insult. It remembers the rule: their land isn't yours, and fear doesn't make it yours. A strong people's power is measured partly by what it walks past.
screen: `ESAU'S CHILDREN: YOUR BROTHERS.` · `NOT EVEN A FOOTSTEP OF LAND.` · `YOU HAVE LACKED NOTHING.` · `MOAB'S LAND WAS GIVEN TOO.` · then, large: `PASS BY GENTLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: leave alone what isn't yours. Settle, and breathe. Think of a place where you have a little power over someone. A younger sibling, a new hire, a neighbor's parking spot, a conversation you could easily take over. Is there something there you've been nudging toward yourself, just because you could? Let the line sit with you: you have lacked nothing. Notice what you actually have. Then picture walking past the thing that isn't yours, without resentment. The bell holds the time.
Devarim. Words, and in them a march where the strong side pays for its water and walks around.
Your line: pass by gently. Today, when you could take a little more than your share, of space, time or credit, walk past it. Day four hundred eighty-six.

howItsDone: This passage is read in synagogues as part of Devarim, the first portion of Deuteronomy, and commentators often point to it as an example of the Torah recognizing the land rights of Israel's neighbors.

trapdoor: what you thought: a travel note on the route to the Jordan.
what it means: the strong are told to walk past land that isn't theirs, and pay for their water, because they lack nothing.
what a scholar hears: Numbers 20:14–21 has Edom refusing passage; Deuteronomy 2 keeps the rule and passes over the insult.
